\section[canis, fēlēs, cattus]{canis, fēlēs, cattus — the expected word, and the word that pushed it out}

\label{lesson:LA-C17-canis-feles-cattus}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} Spanish's \emph{perro} mysteriously displaced the word Latin gave it. Here is that word, and a parallel story about "cat."
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{canis} ("\textbf{dog}") is the direct source of English \textbf{canine}, French \textbf{chien}, Italian \textbf{cane} — and it's also the Latin word Spanish \textbf{inherited} first, as \textbf{can}. But Spanish's everyday word for dog is \emph{perro} instead, a word with \textbf{no confirmed etymology at all} — \emph{can} survives only in archaic or literary use, quietly pushed aside by a newcomer nobody can fully explain.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: fēlēs and cattus — a similar displacement, this time INSIDE Latin}
Here is a parallel that happened \textbf{within Latin itself}, before any Romance language existed:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{fēlēs} was Classical Latin's own, original word for "\textbf{cat}" — used by Cicero, Pliny, and others, and still preserved today in the scientific name for the domestic cat, \emph{\textbf{Felis catus}}.
  \item \textbf{cattus} (also \emph{catta}) is a \textbf{later} word that entered Latin as domestic cats themselves spread along Roman trade routes, out of their point of domestication in \textbf{Egypt} (c. 2000 BCE). \emph{Cattus} is most likely ultimately an \textbf{Afro-Asiatic} word (compare Nubian \emph{kadis}, "cat") — the word traveled \textbf{with the animal}.
\end{itemize}

By around 700 CE, \emph{cattus} had pushed \emph{fēlēs} out of everyday use almost everywhere — it's \emph{cattus}, not \emph{fēlēs}, that gives Spanish \emph{gato}, Italian \emph{gatto}, French \emph{chat}, and more.

\begin{culture}
Both "dog" and "cat" show a Latin-inherited word getting pushed aside by a newcomer — but the two stories aren't equally well understood. \emph{Cattus} replacing \emph{fēlēs} is a well-documented, well-sourced piece of history, with a real trade-route explanation. \emph{Perro} replacing \emph{canis}-derived \emph{can} is genuinely \textbf{unexplained} — a real gap in the historical record, not just a simplification for beginners.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "canis" — dog, source of English "canine"{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "fēlēs" — Classical Latin's own word for cat{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "cattus" — the newcomer that replaced it, probably from Egypt via Africa{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} What English word is a direct cousin of \textbf{canis}? (\textbf{Canine}.) Which Latin word for "cat" is older — \emph{fēlēs} or \emph{cattus}? (\textbf{Fēlēs} — Classical Latin's own word, later displaced.) Where does \emph{cattus} most likely come from? (An \textbf{Afro-Asiatic} word, probably from \textbf{Egypt}, that traveled with the cat itself.) Is Spanish's \emph{perro}-for-\emph{can} displacement just as well understood as Latin's \emph{cattus}-for-\emph{fēlēs} displacement? (\textbf{No} — \emph{cattus} has a real, sourced history; \emph{perro} remains a genuine, unsolved mystery.)
\end{tcolorbox}
